title: How to program for novices (with an hypertrophy bias)
summary: The reasoning behind his novice hypertrophy program. 'Anything works' for novices, but they should build a base with full-ROM compounds, short one-hour sessions three days a week, very low autoregulated loads, and gradually increasing volume, plus small doses of isolation, with the long-term goal of learning to program for themselves.

claims.claim: His programs are built around hypertrophy, not strength or athletic goals, though those follow from gaining muscle.
For novices anything works, but that true saying is misused; because anything works, novices should do things that set up the rest of their journey.
Partial pin presses, hack/behind-the-back squats, pistol squats with bands etc. would all build muscle in a novice but aren't beneficial for building a base.
Novices should build a muscular base that lets them branch out and discover what they like, what they respond to, and what they want to look like; this takes years even though novice status is short.
A novice's goal is a resilient body that moves with proper form and can take on a lot of volume, because size comes with volume.
Beginners can't handle volume: they tire fast, recovery fails, and some even get sick; two extra sets of 10 can wreck a beginner for a week.
By the time you can work out for two hours you will already have an impressive physique.
Knowing how to program for yourself is a milestone as important as, or more than, a 500 lb deadlift.
Novice sessions should last about an hour at most because the gym is an unfamiliar, mentally taxing environment and going too hard early kills motivation.
Give novices just a small taste of the gym each week so they are eager to come back rather than dreading it; the aim is discipline.
Each day starts with a compound with two days between sessions; that's not optimal for frequency, but novices don't need to worry about frequency.
Monday is a knee-flexion compound, Wednesday a pressing compound for chest and shoulders, Friday a hip hinge.
Compounds give the most size in the least time, are hard but necessary, and improve balance and the ability to move through space with weight.
All compounds should be full range of motion; he doesn't believe in novices starting with partials. Go as deep as is comfortable and work toward full depth.
Lifting with imperfect form is OK for novices because loads are very low, making injury risk nearly non-existent.
Beginner programs that add weight every session burn out progression, causing stalls and endless deload cycles, which is terrible mentally.
Start with very low weight and autoregulate: add weight when you feel like it and never let it get too difficult; people who won't push themselves would never gain anyway.
He rejects the simplistic 5x5 add-weight approach: not enough volume, and it teaches novices to be good in only one rep range when they should be good everywhere.
To learn to swim you should be tossed into the sea: beginners should explore rather than repeat the same thing.
Novices should study lifting and get form checks from trusted people, videos, mirrors or YouTube; he taught himself form from YouTube without anyone checking.
The program teaches compounds as the meat and potatoes, how to manipulate them to avoid overuse injuries, and small isolation doses that grow as you target areas you want to develop.
After graduating from the novice program, make it harder or move to the full-body hypertrophy program in his 'natural apogee' playlist.
